title: Lesson 11: Automation and Cron Jobs: Turning One-Off Wins Into Reliable Recurring Value
description: Turning a proven one-off agent win into recurring value on a schedule, with self-contained prompts a fresh session can execute and unattended work that fails loudly instead of silently.

questions.question: Per the lesson about automation and cron jobs, what is the central focus?
options: Turning a proven one-off win into recurring value on a schedule, with self-contained prompts and loud failures
A history of scheduling software and its vendors
A review of unrelated productivity tools
A summary of corporate policy rules
questions.explanation: The lesson centers on turning a proven one-off win into recurring value, writing prompts that survive a fresh run, and making unattended work fail loudly.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the lesson's guidance?
options: A scheduled task that worked once by hand is a candidate even if it needed your judgment at three points
Automate a proven win, never a hope, and never schedule something before it works reliably by hand
Every recurring task should run as a full agent so it can reason
Script-only work is the right default for tasks that need judgment
questions.explanation: The lesson is explicit that you automate a proven win, never a hope, and scheduling before it works by hand just automates failure on a timetable.

questions.question: Which conclusion does the lesson support?
options: Treating it ran as it delivered is safe because a completed run always reaches the recipient
Delivery failures are not a concern for scheduled jobs
A job whose output reaches nobody has not delivered anything, and delivery fails separately from execution
Scheduled runs inherit the context from the conversation that created them
questions.explanation: The lesson teaches that run and delivery fail separately, so a job that produced output nobody saw has delivered nothing.
